concepts.title: RDS: Managed Relational Databases
concepts.description: RDS takes over patching, backups, and failover for a relational database engine you already know, but it draws its own version of the Shared Responsibility line. Knowing what AWS takes over and what you still own keeps a managed database from becoming a false sense of security.
learningObjectives: Explain what RDS automates compared to running the same database engine yourself on EC2, and what remains the customer's responsibility either way.
Explain how RDS Multi-AZ failover works and why it protects availability, not performance or scalability.
Distinguish a Multi-AZ standby from a read replica, including how each is used and what kind of failure or load each one addresses.
Explain automated backups and point-in-time recovery, including their recovery granularity and retention limits.
Diagnose a scenario where an application's read load is the bottleneck versus one where availability is the bottleneck, and choose the correct RDS feature for each.

sections.heading: What RDS Actually Takes Over
sections.body:
Amazon RDS runs a real relational database engine (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2, or AWS's own Aurora), but instead of you installing and operating it on an EC2 instance, AWS provisions and manages the underlying compute and storage. RDS takes over the operating system: you never see or patch a guest OS, and there is no SSH access to a standard RDS instance. It applies engine patches and minor version upgrades in a maintenance window you configure, automates backups, can scale storage, and handles the mechanics of failover for a Multi-AZ deployment (covered below).

This is the Shared Responsibility Model shifting further toward AWS, as introduced earlier in this course. With a self-managed database on EC2 you own OS patching, engine installation and patching, backup automation, and failover orchestration, on top of everything you own with RDS. What RDS does *not* take over: your schema design, query performance and indexing, IAM and database-credential access control, your data's correctness, and your instance sizing and Multi-AZ and read-replica choices. RDS automates the mechanics of the features you turn on, but it does not decide whether you need them or size the instance for your load. A poorly indexed query is as slow on RDS as on a self-managed database on EC2.

sections.heading: Multi-AZ: Automated Failover, Not a Performance Feature
sections.body:
An RDS Multi-AZ deployment maintains a synchronously replicated standby copy of your database in a *different* Availability Zone from the primary, the AZ-diversification principle from the first concept applied to a managed database. Every write to the primary is replicated to the standby before it is acknowledged as durable, so the standby is always caught up, at the cost of some added write latency. If the primary or its whole AZ fails, RDS detects the failure and promotes the standby, typically within roughly 60-120 seconds, and repoints the database's DNS endpoint at the new primary. Your application doesn't need a new connection string, but it must handle a brief connection interruption during the failover, usually with connection retry logic. Build that in instead of assuming failover is instantaneous and invisible. (Cached DNS lookups can lengthen the outage, so keep the DNS TTL in your connection pool low. RDS Proxy can also shorten the application-visible outage by holding connections open across the failover.) You can rehearse this before an incident with `aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier orders-db --force-failover`, which makes the reboot fail over to the standby, so you see how your application behaves.

**Multi-AZ exists for availability, not for performance or read scalability.** In the standard Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the standby serves no read traffic during normal operation. It is a failover target, idle from the application's point of view until it is promoted. A team that enables Multi-AZ expecting it to relieve read load on the primary has misread the feature. Read replicas, covered next, are the separate feature for that, even though both involve extra copies of your data. (RDS also offers a newer Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment for MySQL and PostgreSQL with two readable standbys, and Aurora has its own reader instances. This lesson describes the classic instance deployment.)

sections.heading: Read Replicas: Scaling Read Throughput, Asynchronously
sections.body:
A **read replica** is a separate RDS instance that receives data asynchronously from a source database (unlike a Multi-AZ standby, which is synchronous) and, unlike that standby, *can* serve live read queries. Read-heavy applications can point part of their read traffic (reporting queries, analytics, read-only API endpoints) at one or more replicas, freeing the primary for writes and for reads that need up-to-the-millisecond freshness.

Because replication is asynchronous, there is **replication lag**: a small, variable delay between a write completing on the primary and becoming visible on a replica. It is typically milliseconds but can grow under heavy write load or replica resource contention (the `ReplicaLag` CloudWatch metric tracks it). That makes replicas a poor fit for a read that must see a write made an instant earlier. A user submitting a form and being redirected to a page that reads the record back from a lagging replica may see stale data. That read belongs on the primary, or needs an application-level strategy to tolerate the lag. Read replicas can also be promoted to standalone databases, which helps when splitting off a workload or in disaster recovery scenarios that differ from Multi-AZ's automated same-Region failover. A replica can even be created in a *different* Region than its source, which a Multi-AZ standby cannot, so cross-Region replicas address a different kind of resilience than in-Region Multi-AZ failover. MySQL, MariaDB, and PostgreSQL instances support up to 15 replicas each. Each replica is a full instance with its own cost, and replicas do not help write throughput at all, since every write still lands on the primary.

sections.heading: Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery: What They Actually Restore, and How Far Back
sections.body:
RDS automated backups take a daily snapshot of the database and continuously capture transaction logs. Together these enable **point-in-time recovery (PITR)**: restoring the database to its state at any second within the retention window (up to 35 days), not just to the moment of the last daily snapshot. During an incident this matters: if a bad deployment or an accidental `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause corrupts data at 2:17pm, PITR lets you restore to 2:16pm instead of losing a day of legitimate writes by rolling back to last night's snapshot.

This detail causes bad surprises during real incidents: a PITR restore does not modify the existing database. It creates a **new** RDS instance at the recovered point in time, with a new endpoint. Recovering from a bad write means restoring to a new instance, verifying the data there, and then redirecting the application to it (or exporting and re-applying the corrected data). It is not an in-place undo. Automated backups also have a finite retention window, up to 35 days, and they are deleted when you delete the instance unless you choose to retain them. Longer retention (regulatory rules, year-over-year archival) needs **snapshots** that you take and keep deliberately, manually or through AWS Backup. The CLI offers a shortcut for the most recent recoverable moment: `--use-latest-restorable-time` in place of `--restore-time`.

sections.heading: What Still Isn't RDS's Job: Schema, Queries, Sizing, and Access Control
sections.body:
Assuming a managed service has taken over more than it has is a recurring failure mode, so it helps to mark where RDS's automation stops. RDS does not design your schema or choose your indexes, and it runs a poorly written query or an unindexed table scan as slowly as a self-managed database would. Query and schema performance sit on the 'in the cloud' side of the line, however much infrastructure AWS manages. RDS also does not size your instance for you: an undersized instance class bottlenecks on CPU, memory, or IOPS however well patched and backed up it is, and choosing the instance class and storage configuration is the customer's decision, like the EC2 family choice covered earlier.

Access control follows the same pattern. RDS integrates with IAM for *administrative* actions (creating, modifying, deleting an instance) and optionally for authenticating to the database through IAM database authentication, but the database's internal user and permission model (`GRANT`/`REVOKE`, or the engine's equivalent) is yours to design and maintain, as on a self-managed database. A security group that is too permissive, or a database user with broader privileges than the application needs, is an 'in the cloud' misconfiguration that RDS's automation does nothing to prevent. Keep the master password out of scripts: `--manage-master-user-password` lets RDS store and rotate it in Secrets Manager. The managed service took patching and failover off your plate, not the job of configuring access correctly.

examples.title: Creating a Multi-AZ RDS Instance and Adding a Read Replica
examples.code:
# A Multi-AZ primary: the standby is created and kept in sync automatically,
# but is not available for read queries.
# '**********' is a placeholder; in practice prefer --manage-master-user-password
# so the password lives in Secrets Manager instead of a shell history.
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --engine postgres \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large \
  --allocated-storage 100 \
  --multi-az \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password '**********'

# A read replica of that same database, usable for live read queries,
# receiving data asynchronously with some replication lag
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier orders-db-read-1 \
  --source-db-instance-identifier orders-db
examples.explanation: These two commands create two different things that are easy to conflate because both involve 'another copy of the database'. The `--multi-az` flag gives the primary a synchronously replicated standby for automated failover; it can't be queried and adds nothing to read capacity. `create-db-instance-read-replica` creates a separate, independently addressable instance (`orders-db-read-1`, with its own endpoint) that an application can send read queries to, kept in sync asynchronously. A team that runs only the first command and then wonders why read-heavy dashboard queries still bottleneck on the primary has set up availability but not read scalability. Neither command substitutes for the other.

examples.title: Point-in-Time Recovery After a Bad Write
examples.code:
# A bad deployment ran an UPDATE without a WHERE clause at 14:17 UTC,
# corrupting the orders table. Restore to just before that moment --
# NOTE: this creates a brand-new instance, it does not modify orders-db in place.
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time \
  --source-db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --target-db-instance-identifier orders-db-restored-14-16 \
  --restore-time 2026-08-14T14:16:00Z
examples.explanation: This command produces a new RDS instance, `orders-db-restored-14-16`, rebuilt from the automated backup and transaction logs to match `orders-db` at 14:16:00 UTC, one minute before the bad update. The original `orders-db` is untouched and keeps serving traffic, corrupted data included, while you verify the restored instance and decide what to do (redirect the application to it, or copy the corrected rows back). Internalize this before an incident, not during one: point-in-time recovery creates a new, correct instance next to the broken one. It is not an undo button on the production database. The restored instance also comes up with default parameter and security group settings unless you specify them, so check those before cutting traffic over.

examples.title: A Correctly-Sized Instance Still Bottlenecked by a Missing Index
examples.code:
-- (illustrative output) orders table: 40 million rows, no index on customer_id
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 48213;

-- Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..812000.00 rows=12 width=96)
--   Filter: (customer_id = 48213)
--   Rows Removed by Filter: 39999988
--   Execution Time: 4210.331 ms

-- After: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 48213;

-- Index Scan using idx_orders_customer_id on orders  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=12)
--   Index Cond: (customer_id = 48213)
--   Execution Time: 0.412 ms
examples.explanation: This query runs on a properly sized, Multi-AZ, automatically backed-up RDS instance, so every operational box RDS owns is checked. Yet the first version takes over 4 seconds, because PostgreSQL has no index to use and scans all 40 million rows (the `Rows Removed by Filter` line shows the waste), and RDS's patching and failover have no bearing on that. Adding the index drops execution time to under half a millisecond, roughly a 10,000x improvement, through index design alone. That responsibility sits with the customer on any platform, RDS or self-managed. Operational automation and query performance are independent axes, and excellence on one says nothing about the other.

misconceptions.description: Enabling Multi-AZ on an RDS instance improves read performance by letting the application spread queries across the primary and the standby.
misconceptions.clarification: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the standby is a synchronously replicated failover target and cannot serve read queries during normal operation. It sits idle, from the application's perspective, until RDS promotes it after detecting a primary failure. Spreading reads across instances requires read replicas, a separate feature that creates independently queryable instances kept in sync asynchronously. Enabling Multi-AZ addresses availability; it does nothing for read throughput.
misconceptions.fact: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the standby exists as a synchronously replicated failover target and cannot serve read queries during normal operation.

misconceptions.description: Because RDS handles patching, backups, and failover automatically, a team no longer needs to think about database performance or access control -- those are 'AWS's problem' once the database is on RDS.
misconceptions.clarification: RDS automates the operational mechanics of running the engine (OS patching, engine updates, backup scheduling, failover orchestration), but schema design, query and index performance, instance sizing for the load, and access control (IAM for administrative actions and the database's own user and permission model) remain the customer's responsibility, as on a self-managed database. A poorly indexed query or an overly permissive database user is as real a problem on RDS as anywhere else. RDS's automation covers infrastructure operations, not application correctness or performance.

exercises.prompt: A team enabled Multi-AZ on their production RDS instance specifically to fix slow response times on their read-heavy reporting dashboard, reasoning that the standby instance could absorb some of that read load. Response times haven't improved at all. Diagnose why, and propose the actual fix.
exercises.code:
current_setup:
  db_instance: orders-db
  multi_az: true          # enabled specifically hoping to offload read traffic
  read_replicas: []       # none configured
  symptom: "reporting dashboard queries still slow, no change after enabling Multi-AZ"
hints: What is a Multi-AZ standby available for during normal operation? Can an application send it read queries?
The feature that creates an additional, independently queryable copy of the data for read traffic is a different RDS feature entirely from Multi-AZ.
Consider also whether reporting/dashboard queries specifically need up-to-the-second freshness, or whether they could tolerate the small replication lag that comes with the correct fix.
exercises.solutionCode:
fixed_setup:
  db_instance: orders-db
  multi_az: true                     # keep -- this still correctly protects availability
  read_replicas: ["orders-db-read-1"]  # add -- this is what actually offloads read traffic
  dashboard_queries_routed_to: "orders-db-read-1"
exercises.solutionExplanation: Multi-AZ's standby is not available for query traffic during normal operation, since it exists as a synchronously replicated failover target, so enabling it changes nothing about read capacity or latency. That is why the dashboard saw no improvement. The fix is a read replica, a separate RDS feature that creates an independently addressable instance fed asynchronously, with the reporting queries pointed at the replica's endpoint instead of the primary's. Multi-AZ should stay on, since it still protects availability against an AZ or instance failure, but it was never designed to solve a read-throughput problem.

exercises.prompt: At 09:00 UTC, a deploy script accidentally runs an UPDATE that corrupts pricing data across an entire product catalog table. The team notices at 09:45 UTC and immediately runs a point-in-time-recovery restore targeting 08:59 UTC. Describe exactly what state the production system is in immediately after that restore command completes, and what manual steps (if any) remain before the corrupted data is actually fixed for real users.
exercises.code:
timeline:
  09:00 UTC: bad UPDATE runs, corrupting pricing data
  09:45 UTC: team notices, initiates PITR restore targeting 08:59 UTC
  restore command: aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time --source-db-instance-identifier catalog-db --target-db-instance-identifier catalog-db-restored --restore-time 2026-08-14T08:59:00Z
hints: PITR restores create a new instance rather than modifying the existing one in place -- what is catalog-db (the original, currently-serving instance) doing throughout this whole process?
The new instance, catalog-db-restored, has correct pricing data as of 08:59 UTC -- but is it the instance real users' traffic is actually reaching right after the restore command finishes?
Think about what legitimate writes (new orders, inventory changes, etc.) might have happened on catalog-db between 08:59 and 09:45 that also aren't reflected on the restored instance.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Immediately after the restore command completes, catalog-db (the original instance) is still running and still serving live production traffic, with the corrupted pricing data from the 09:00 UPDATE still present -- the restore command did not touch it. A new, separate instance, catalog-db-restored, now exists with correct pricing data as of 08:59 UTC, but nothing is pointed at it yet. Real users are not yet seeing correct data. Manual steps remain: verify catalog-db-restored has the expected correct data, reconcile any legitimate writes that happened between 08:59 and 09:45 (which exist on catalog-db but not on the restored instance) so they aren't lost, and then either redirect the application to catalog-db-restored or selectively copy the corrected pricing rows back into catalog-db.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time` always creates a brand-new RDS instance instead of modifying the source, so when the command finishes there are two databases: the original `catalog-db`, unchanged and still serving traffic with the corrupted pricing, and `catalog-db-restored`, holding everything as of 08:59 UTC. Running the restore redirects no traffic, so real users still see the corrupted state: the restore produced a correct *copy*, not a live fix. (The restore also takes time to provision, so the new instance may not even be available yet when the command returns.) The 46-minute gap between 08:59 and 09:45 matters too: legitimate order or inventory changes made on `catalog-db` in that window don't exist on `catalog-db-restored`, so a full cutover without reconciling the gap would lose valid data along with the corruption. Verifying the restored data and reconciling the gap are necessary manual steps, not a formality.

assessments.prompt: A team's RDS-hosted application is experiencing slow read query performance during peak hours, and a review shows the primary instance's CPU is consistently near 100% due to heavy analytical reporting queries mixed in with normal transactional traffic. Which RDS feature most directly addresses this specific bottleneck?
options: Switching the database engine from the current engine to a different one, since engine choice determines CPU capacity.
Enabling Multi-AZ, so the standby instance can absorb some of the reporting query load.
Adding one or more read replicas and routing the analytical reporting queries to them.
Increasing the automated backup retention period to capture more historical data for reporting purposes.
assessments.explanation: The bottleneck, primary CPU saturated by a mix of transactional and analytical queries, is what read replicas relieve: routing reporting queries to replicas frees the primary's CPU for transactional traffic, at the cost of a small replication lag that is usually acceptable for reporting. The “Enabling Multi-AZ, so the standby instance can…” option is the classic Multi-AZ misconception -- a standby cannot serve any query traffic at all during normal operation, so it does nothing for this bottleneck. The “Increasing the automated backup retention period…” option confuses backup retention (how far back you can restore to) with query capacity, which are unrelated. The “Switching the database engine from the current…” option is a red herring: CPU capacity depends on instance class and size, not on the engine, and switching engines is a disproportionate response to a workload-distribution problem.

assessments.prompt: During an RDS Multi-AZ failover, the database's DNS endpoint automatically updates to point at the newly promoted standby, with the whole process typically completing within roughly 60-120 seconds. Given this, what should application code do to handle a failover gracefully?
options: Switch the application to use a read replica's endpoint instead of the primary's, since only read replicas remain reachable during a Multi-AZ failover.
Nothing; failover is instantaneous and completely invisible to any application already connected to the database.
Manually reconfigure the application's connection string to a new endpoint once failover completes, since the DNS endpoint does not update on its own.
Implement connection retry logic to handle the brief connection interruption during the failover window.
assessments.explanation: RDS updates the DNS endpoint automatically during a Multi-AZ failover, so the application never needs a new connection string, but the failover is not invisible: existing connections are dropped while the standby is promoted and the application must reconnect, which is why retry logic matters. The “Nothing; failover is instantaneous and completely invisible…” option overstates the guarantee -- there's a real, if brief, disruption window. The “Manually reconfigure the application's connection string…” option is wrong because the DNS endpoint update is automatic, not manual. The “Switch the application to use a read…” option confuses read replicas (a separate feature for read scaling) with the Multi-AZ standby itself, which is what actually gets promoted during this specific failover.

assessments.prompt: A user submits a form that writes a new record to the primary RDS instance, and the application immediately redirects them to a page that reads that same record back from a read replica. What is the most likely risk, and why?
options: The read might not find the record yet, or might see a stale version of it, because replication to a read replica is asynchronous, introducing replication lag between when a write completes on the primary and when it becomes visible on that replica.
There is no risk; read replicas are updated synchronously, so the new record is guaranteed to be visible immediately.
This is only a risk if Multi-AZ happens to also be enabled on the same primary instance.
The read will fail outright, since read replicas cannot serve any read traffic for the first several seconds after any write occurs anywhere in the database.
assessments.explanation: Read replicas receive data asynchronously, unlike a Multi-AZ standby's synchronous replication, which means there's a small, variable replication lag between a write completing on the primary and that write becoming visible on a given replica. Writing to the primary and immediately reading from a replica (read-your-own-write) is the case where that lag surfaces as a visible bug, with stale or missing data. The “There is no risk; read replicas…” option incorrectly attributes synchronous replication to read replicas, which is the Multi-AZ standby's behavior, not a read replica's. The “The read will fail outright, since read…” option invents an outright failure mode that doesn't reflect how replication lag actually behaves -- reads still succeed, they just may return stale data. The “This is only a risk if Multi-AZ…” option incorrectly ties this risk to Multi-AZ, which is an unrelated, separate feature.

assessments.prompt: A company needs to retain the ability to restore their RDS database to any specific point in time within the last 2 years, for a regulatory retention requirement. Is RDS's automated backup and point-in-time recovery feature sufficient for this on its own?
options: Yes, automated backups and point-in-time recovery support an effectively unlimited retention window by default.
No -- automated backups' point-in-time recovery window has a maximum retention of up to 35 days.
No, because RDS provides no backup or recovery capability of any kind beyond whatever a read replica happens to retain.
Yes, as long as Multi-AZ is enabled, since the standby instance retains historical data indefinitely.
assessments.explanation: RDS automated backups and point-in-time recovery have a finite retention window of up to 35 days, so a 2-year regulatory requirement is well beyond what that feature provides alone. Longer retention requires snapshots (manual, or scheduled through AWS Backup) taken and kept deliberately as a separate archival policy. The “Yes, automated backups and point-in-time recovery support…” option overstates the retention window, which is explicitly capped. The “Yes, as long as Multi-AZ is enabled…” option incorrectly attributes indefinite historical retention to the Multi-AZ standby, which only mirrors current data for failover purposes and isn't a historical archive. The “No, because RDS provides no backup…” option understates RDS's real, genuine backup capability, which does exist -- it's just capped well short of 2 years.

assessments.prompt: A junior engineer says, 'We moved our database to RDS, so we don't really need to worry about database performance or security anymore -- AWS manages it.' Explain what's accurate and what's mistaken in that statement, being specific about where the actual dividing line falls.
assessments.modelAnswer: The accurate part deserves credit: RDS takes over a large category of operational work that a self-managed database would leave to the team. It patches the guest OS (which RDS users never access), applies engine updates on a schedule, automates daily backups and transaction-log capture for point-in-time recovery, and orchestrates Multi-AZ failover. The team writes and maintains no tooling for any of that, which is a meaningful reduction in burden. The mistake is treating 'AWS manages the infrastructure' as 'AWS manages our outcomes.' Schema design and query performance are untouched by RDS's automation: an unindexed query scanning forty million rows runs as slowly on a patched, backed-up RDS instance as anywhere else, because that is a property of the schema and the query, not the infrastructure. Instance sizing is the same story: RDS will run whatever instance class is selected, but it doesn't decide whether that class is actually sufficient for the real workload, and an undersized instance bottlenecks on CPU, memory, or IOPS regardless of how well-managed its patching is. Security follows the same pattern: RDS integrates with IAM for administrative actions and can support IAM database authentication, but the database's own grants and the security groups controlling network access are the team's configuration to get right. An overly permissive database user or an open security group is as real a vulnerability on RDS as on a self-managed instance, and RDS's automation does not catch it. Check also that the instance is not publicly accessible unless it has to be (`--no-publicly-accessible`) and that its security group admits only the application tier. So RDS moved one well-defined category of work, infrastructure operations, to AWS's side of the line, and left schema design, query performance, instance sizing, and access control with the team, as consequential as ever.

concepts.title: DynamoDB Basics: Keys, Partitions, and NoSQL Scaling
concepts.description: DynamoDB stores items addressed by a key rather than rows related through joins. Its partition key is the design decision that decides whether the table scales smoothly to massive throughput or concentrates traffic on one overloaded partition, which is why DynamoDB rewards designing access patterns up front in a way relational databases don't require.
learningObjectives: Explain DynamoDB's item/attribute data model and contrast it with a relational table's rows and columns, including why DynamoDB has no joins.
Explain what a partition key is, how DynamoDB uses it to distribute data and throughput, and why key choice directly determines scalability.
Diagnose a 'hot partition' problem from its symptoms and propose a partition key redesign that fixes it.
Distinguish a simple primary key from a composite primary key (partition key + sort key) and explain what a sort key enables.
Explain why DynamoDB scales differently from a relational database: why key-based access doesn't get slower as a table grows, provided the partition key is well chosen.

sections.heading: Items and Attributes, Not Rows and Columns -- and No Joins
sections.body:
A DynamoDB table stores **items**, and each item is a collection of **attributes**, similar to a JSON document: DynamoDB natively supports nested lists and maps as attribute values, not just flat scalars. Unlike a relational table, items in one DynamoDB table needn't share the same attributes. One item might have five attributes and the next a different eight, with no schema migration, because DynamoDB enforces a schema only for the key attributes that identify each item.

The bigger difference is that **DynamoDB has no joins**. That is a deliberate constraint that shapes how you use the service. A relational database lets you normalize data across tables and reassemble it at query time with a `JOIN`. DynamoDB expects you to model data so that everything an access pattern needs comes from one table (often one item, or a small predictable set of items under one partition key) in one request, because nothing combines items at query time the way a join combines rows. This moves design work earlier than a relational schema does: you need to know your actual access patterns, which queries you'll run and how often, *before* finalizing the table and key design, and denormalize and duplicate data where needed so each pattern becomes an efficient read without joins. Teams that arrive with a relational mindset, normalize as they would in Postgres, and then wonder how to 'join' later hit one of the most common early missteps with the service.

sections.heading: The Partition Key: What Actually Determines Scalability
sections.body:
Every DynamoDB table has a **partition key** (also called a hash key), and DynamoDB uses it to decide which physical storage partition an item lives on: the key's value goes through an internal hash function, and the result determines placement. This mechanism is the basis of DynamoDB's scaling to very large request volumes. As traffic grows, DynamoDB can add partitions behind the scenes and spread load across them, provided the load is spread across many *distinct partition key values* to begin with.

That last clause is the catch, and it causes the most common DynamoDB design mistake, a **hot partition**. If much of a table's traffic concentrates on a few partition key values (a status field with only three values such as `"pending"`, `"active"`, `"closed"` used as the partition key, or one tenant ID that accounts for a disproportionate share of traffic), then however many partitions the table has been split into, that key's traffic is confined to the one partition its value hashes to. A single partition supports at most about 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second, and requests above that are throttled even while the table's *aggregate* provisioned or on-demand capacity looks nowhere near exhausted. The symptom is confusing because table-wide dashboards can look healthy while one access pattern is throttled hard. Reads also default to eventual consistency (a `GetItem` or `Query` may briefly miss a very recent write unless you pass `ConsistentRead=true`), a lighter echo of the replica-lag trade-off from the RDS concept. (DynamoDB's adaptive capacity softens this by rebalancing and isolating busy items, but it cannot raise the per-key ceiling, so one key that needs more than 1,000 writes per second is still a design problem.) The fix is a partition key whose values are numerous and appear with roughly even frequency in real traffic. A customer ID or order ID suits a workload with many customers or orders far better than a low-cardinality status field, because it spreads across many partitions.

sections.heading: Composite Primary Keys: Adding a Sort Key
sections.body:
A table defines either a **simple primary key** (the partition key alone, uniquely identifying each item) or a **composite primary key** (a partition key plus a **sort key**). The sort key adds query capability, not just a second identifying field. Within one partition key value, items are stored sorted by sort key, so a query for 'all items with this partition key where the sort key falls in this range' is efficient and native, with no scan.

A common pattern: a table with partition key `customerId` and sort key `orderDate#orderId` lets one `Query` fetch all orders for a customer in chronological order, or within a date range. The composite key does the work of a relational `WHERE customer_id = ? AND order_date BETWEEN ? AND ?` with an index, expressed through key design. DynamoDB also supports separate **secondary indexes**, global and local, for access patterns that don't fit the primary key; they are the escape hatch when one key structure can't serve every access pattern. Without a sort key, a partition key value identifies exactly one item, so there is no 'range of items under the same partition key' at all.

sections.heading: Why DynamoDB Scales Differently From a Relational Database
sections.body:
In a well-designed DynamoDB table, the latency of a key-based read or write stays roughly constant as the table grows. Fetching one item by its exact primary key takes about the same time with a thousand items or a hundred billion, because DynamoDB routes the request to the partition holding the item without searching unrelated data. A relational database differs: an unindexed query's cost grows with the *total* table size (recall the 40-million-row sequential scan that took over four seconds in the RDS concept). Indexes mitigate that, while DynamoDB builds the property into its model by using the partition key as the address for every request instead of as an optional optimization on top of a scannable table.

The trade-off is that this speed is available for queries that go through the partition key (and, within a partition, the sort key). A request that doesn't specify the partition key and filters on some other attribute needs a `Scan`, which reads through a large part or all of the table. That is slow and expensive at scale, just like a relational full-table scan, and AWS advises against relying on it for tables of any real size. This is the payoff of designing around access patterns up front: a table modeled around the queries the application runs gets fast, scale-independent performance, while a table queried in ways its keys weren't designed for falls back to the scanning cost profile DynamoDB was built to avoid.

examples.title: Modeling One Access Pattern With a Composite Key
examples.explanation: The sort key `ORDER#2026-08-01#O-9911` puts the order date before the order ID, a common modeling technique so that a range condition on the sort key (`begins_with`, or `BETWEEN` on a date range) expresses 'orders in this date range', since items under one partition key are stored sorted by sort key. An item retrieved by one `Query` contains everything this access pattern needs: there is no second table to join for line items, because they are embedded as a nested list instead of normalized into a separate table as a relational schema would. This is the denormalization described earlier: the data is shaped around 'fetch a customer's orders in a date range, with line items', not around a join-friendly structure. The trade-off is item size: a single item is limited to 400 KB, so an unbounded list (every event ever for a user) should be separate items under the same partition key, not one growing attribute. In a real call, `total` and `status` are DynamoDB reserved words, so expressions that reference them need placeholders such as `#t`.

examples.title: A Hot Partition, Diagnosed From Symptoms
examples.code:
Table: Jobs   partition key: status   (values: "pending", "processing", "done")

CloudWatch metrics:
  Table-level ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits: well within provisioned capacity
  WriteThrottleEvents: spiking heavily
  CloudWatch Contributor Insights (most throttled keys): "pending" accounts for
    nearly all throttled requests; "done" is near zero

Symptom: workers polling for status="pending" jobs get throttled constantly,
while the table's overall metrics look healthy.
examples.explanation: This is the hot-partition symptom made concrete. The partition key is `status`, which takes only three values however large the table grows. Every 'pending' job, potentially millions under load, lives on the one partition the string `"pending"` hashes to, and that partition has its own throughput ceiling independent of the table's aggregate capacity. Table-wide metrics look fine because aggregate traffic across all partitions, including the much lighter `"done"` traffic, is within capacity, while the problem sits in one partition that table-wide totals hide. Per-key metrics are not in the standard table metrics, which is why Contributor Insights is the tool for finding the offending key. The fix is a higher-cardinality partition key such as `jobId`, with `status` as a regular attribute (queried through a secondary index if 'all pending jobs' must stay efficient; note that an index keyed only on `status` would have the same hot-key problem, so it needs a sharded or time-bucketed key). Job traffic then spreads across many partitions instead of collapsing onto three.

examples.title: The Same Table Queried Correctly vs. Via an Expensive Scan
examples.explanation: Both operations can return correct results, but their cost profiles differ, depending on whether the partition key routes the operation. The `Query` goes to the one partition holding `CUST#48213`'s items, so its cost depends on how much data that customer has, not on the size of the `Orders` table. The `Scan` has no partition key to route by, so DynamoDB examines a broad swath of the table to evaluate `total > 100`, and the cost (read capacity consumed is based on the data read, before the filter is applied) grows with table size, not with the number of matches. A `Scan` returning a handful of items from a hundred-million-item table still pays for reading most of the table. That is why designing around access patterns up front matters: a pattern that maps to a `Query` gets DynamoDB's scaling promise, and one that only maps to a `Scan` gets the cost profile the service was designed to avoid.

misconceptions.description: Since DynamoDB is a NoSQL/document database, the choice of partition key is mostly a stylistic preference, similar to picking which column to use as a primary key in a relational table.
misconceptions.clarification: The partition key determines how DynamoDB distributes an item's data and throughput across partitions, and it is the biggest factor in whether a table scales smoothly or develops a hot partition. A low-cardinality partition key (only a handful of distinct values in real traffic) concentrates requests onto very few partitions, each with its own throughput ceiling, whatever the table's overall provisioned or on-demand capacity. It is a scalability decision with operational consequences, not a stylistic choice like picking a relational primary key column.
misconceptions.fact: The partition key choice directly determines how DynamoDB physically distributes an item's data and throughput across its underlying partitions, and it is the single biggest factor in whether a table scales smoothly or develops a hot partition.

misconceptions.description: DynamoDB tables should be modeled the same way relational tables are -- normalize related data into separate tables, then join or query across them as needed at read time.
misconceptions.clarification: DynamoDB has no join operation, and its performance model rewards designing a table (or a few tables) around the application's known access patterns up front, denormalizing and duplicating data so that each pattern is satisfied from one table, often with a single Query, without combining items or tables at query time. Expecting to reassemble normalized data at read time leads to multiple round trips or to expensive Scans.

exercises.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS application stores usage events in a DynamoDB table with partition key tenantTier (values: "free", "pro", "enterprise"). One giant enterprise customer generates the overwhelming majority of all events in the system. The team is seeing throttled writes specifically for enterprise-tier events, even though the table's overall provisioned capacity metrics look far from exhausted. Diagnose the root cause and propose a partition key redesign.
exercises.code:
table: UsageEvents
partition_key: tenantTier   # "free" | "pro" | "enterprise"
symptom: "enterprise-tier writes throttled heavily; table-wide capacity metrics look healthy"
context: "one very large enterprise customer accounts for most of all events system-wide"
hints: How many distinct values can tenantTier take across the whole table, no matter how many tenants or events exist?

Every item with tenantTier = "enterprise", across every enterprise customer including the dominant one, has the same partition key value and so lands on the same partition, regardless of the table's total provisioned capacity.
The fix needs a partition key with much higher cardinality that still supports the application's actual access patterns -- consider using something tenant-specific rather than tier-specific.
exercises.solutionCode:
table: UsageEvents
partition_key: tenantId    # one distinct value per tenant, much higher cardinality
sort_key: eventTimestamp#eventId
# tenantTier moves to a regular (non-key) attribute, queryable via a
# secondary index if "all enterprise-tier events across tenants" is
# still a needed access pattern
exercises.solutionExplanation: `tenantTier` has three possible values, so every item, across all tenants sharing a tier, is stored under one of only three partition key values, and the giant enterprise customer's traffic is confined to the partition `"enterprise"` hashes to, however much capacity the table has. That is a textbook hot partition: the throttling is specific to that partition's throughput ceiling while table-wide metrics, which aggregate the much lighter `"free"` and `"pro"` traffic, look healthy. Switching the partition key to `tenantId` gives every tenant its own partition key value, so traffic distributes by tenant. The dominant tenant still generates a lot of traffic, but it no longer shares a ceiling with every other enterprise-tier tenant. (If that single tenant alone exceeds about 1,000 writes per second, `tenantId` is still not enough, and you would add a shard suffix such as `tenantId#0` to `tenantId#9` and spread its writes across them.) If 'all enterprise-tier events across every tenant' is still a genuinely needed query, that access pattern would now go through a secondary index on the `tenantTier` attribute rather than through the primary key, since the primary key's job has shifted to optimizing for the far more common per-tenant access pattern.

exercises.prompt: Design a partition key and sort key for a DynamoDB table storing chat messages, given this single required access pattern: fetch all messages in a specific chat room, ordered from oldest to newest, optionally limited to a specific date range. Write the key schema and a short example item, then explain why this schema satisfies the access pattern efficiently.
hints: The partition key should be whatever the access pattern always filters down to first. What does every relevant query have in common ("messages in a specific ___")?
The sort key needs to support ordering AND range filtering by date -- what value, placed at the front of the sort key, makes both of those possible via begins_with or a BETWEEN condition?

Make sure the partition key has enough distinct values across the whole table (many chat rooms) to avoid concentrating traffic onto too few partitions, unlike the tenantTier mistake from the previous exercise.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `roomId` is the partition key because the access pattern always filters to 'messages in a specific chat room', and a real application has many rooms, so the key has high cardinality and spreads traffic across partitions, avoiding the previous exercise's mistake. (A single huge room could still run hot, in which case you would bucket it, for example by day.) The sort key `sentAt#messageId` puts an ISO-8601 timestamp first, so items in one room are stored in chronological order, which gives 'oldest to newest' with no extra sorting, and a date range becomes a `BETWEEN` condition on the sort key instead of a filter pass over unrelated items. ISO-8601 timestamps in a single format and timezone sort correctly as strings. The `messageId` suffix guarantees uniqueness if two messages share a timestamp. In a real call, a sort key name containing `#` has to go through `ExpressionAttributeNames`, and many designs use a plain name like `sk` instead. The schema satisfies the one access pattern with a single `Query`, because the pattern was designed into the keys from the start.

assessments.prompt: A DynamoDB table's write requests are being throttled for one specific, very common partition key value, even though CloudWatch shows the table's overall consumed capacity well below its provisioned capacity (or on-demand limits). What does this most strongly indicate?
options: The sort key is missing from the table, which is required for DynamoDB to distribute any table's write load.
DynamoDB is experiencing a regional outage affecting only that specific key value.
The table's total item count has exceeded a hard DynamoDB size limit and needs to be split into multiple tables.

A hot partition: too much traffic is concentrated on that one partition key value, exceeding that specific partition's own throughput ceiling even though aggregate table-wide capacity is not exhausted.
assessments.explanation: Healthy table-wide capacity metrics with throttling on one key value is the defining symptom of a hot partition: DynamoDB distributes items and throughput by the hash of the partition key, and every item sharing one overrepresented key value lands on the same partition, which has its own throughput ceiling independent of the table's aggregate capacity. The “The table's total item count has exceeded…” option invents a size-based limit that isn't the actual mechanism here -- this is a distribution problem, not a total-size problem. The “DynamoDB is experiencing a regional outage affecting…” option fabricates a per-key outage, which isn't how DynamoDB throttling works. The “The sort key is missing…” option is incorrect because a sort key is optional and orthogonal to load distribution -- distribution across partitions is entirely a function of the partition key, not whether a sort key exists.

assessments.prompt: A table has partition key customerId and sort key orderDate#orderId. If this table had only a simple primary key (customerId alone, with no sort key), what specific capability would it lose?
options: The ability to choose between provisioned and on-demand capacity modes for the table.
The ability for the table to distribute items across more than one physical partition at all.
The ability to fetch a range of items sharing the same partition key value.
The ability to store more than one non-key attribute on each item.
assessments.explanation: A sort key lets multiple items share a partition key value while remaining individually addressable and range-queryable, since items within a partition are stored sorted by sort key. Without one, a partition key value maps to exactly one item, so fetching a customer's orders in a date range couldn't be expressed as a single efficient request. The “The ability to store more than one…” option is unrelated -- attribute count per item has nothing to do with sort keys. The “The ability for the table to distribute…” option is wrong -- partition distribution is governed by the partition key alone, independent of whether a sort key exists. The “The ability to choose between provisioned…” option is also unrelated -- capacity mode is a separate table-level setting with no connection to key schema.

assessments.prompt: A DynamoDB table grows from 1 million to 100 million items. A Query using one customer's exact partition key, and a Scan filtering on a non-key attribute across the whole table, are each run before and after this growth. What happens to each operation's latency?
options: Both operations get faster, since DynamoDB automatically adding more partitions as a table grows uniformly speeds up every kind of read, including Scans.

The Query's latency stays roughly the same, since it's routed directly to the one partition holding that customer's items regardless of the table's total size; the Scan's latency grows substantially, since it has to examine a portion of the table proportional to the table's new, much larger size.
Both operations get proportionally slower, since DynamoDB latency is always a direct function of total table size regardless of which operation is used.
The Query becomes slower while the Scan's latency stays constant, since Scans always execute against a fixed-size sample regardless of table size.
assessments.explanation: A Query addressed by an exact partition key is routed to the partition holding that data, so its cost depends on how much data lives under that key, not on table size, which is the scale-independence DynamoDB provides for key-addressed access. A Scan has no partition key to route by, so it examines a portion of the table proportional to total size to evaluate the filter, and its cost grows with the table however few items match. The “Both operations get proportionally slower, since DynamoDB…” option incorrectly generalizes the Scan's size-dependent cost to the Query as well. The “Both operations get faster, since DynamoDB automatically…” option invents a uniform speedup that doesn't apply to Scans, which read broadly regardless of partition count. The “The Query becomes slower while the Scan's…” option reverses which operation is size-independent.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a developer coming from a relational database background why DynamoDB requires knowing your access patterns before finalizing a table design, in a way relational schema design typically doesn't -- and connect this directly to why partition key choice matters so much.
assessments.modelAnswer: A relational database lets you design a normalized schema largely independent of the queries you'll run, because the engine reassembles data at read time with joins and indexes added later make many query shapes efficient without redesigning tables. DynamoDB removes that flexibility on purpose: there is no join, so any access pattern that needs data from multiple items or tables must be served by data already denormalized into one item or partition, or fall back to an expensive Scan. That is why DynamoDB modeling asks you to list your actual access patterns before finalizing the design, instead of designing a natural normalized shape and figuring out queries later. The partition key is the most consequential decision in that process because it affects more than correctness: it determines physical data distribution and therefore scalability. Every item is routed to a specific physical partition based on a hash of its partition key value, and every partition has its own individual throughput ceiling; a partition key with only a few distinct values that actually appear in real traffic concentrates a large share of requests onto very few partitions no matter how much total capacity the table is provisioned with, producing the throttled-but-table-looks-healthy symptom that's the hallmark of a hot partition. A relational primary key has no equivalent physical-distribution consequence at all -- picking one column over another as the primary key doesn't determine how the database engine spreads load across its underlying storage the way a DynamoDB partition key does. So the two pieces connect directly: knowing your access patterns up front tells you which attribute or attributes need to support efficient, joinless retrieval, and picking a partition key with genuinely high cardinality relative to your real traffic -- not just any unique-sounding field -- is what turns that retrieval efficiency into actual, even scalability rather than a design that silently concentrates load onto a handful of overloaded partitions.

concepts.title: Choosing the Right AWS Data Store for the Access Pattern
concepts.description: RDS, DynamoDB, and S3 are not interchangeable options ranked by preference -- each is built around a different access pattern, and picking correctly means starting from how the data will actually be read and written, not from which service is newest or most talked about.
learningObjectives: Articulate the core access-pattern question that should drive a data store choice, before considering any specific AWS service.
Match a described workload to RDS, DynamoDB, or S3 based on its actual read/write/query requirements, not surface-level familiarity or trend.
Explain why relational flexibility (ad-hoc joins and queries) and DynamoDB's scalability are in real tension, and why you can't costlessly get both from the same store.
Identify when a single workload genuinely needs more than one data store working together, and describe a concrete example of that pattern.
Critique a data-store choice made for the wrong reason (trend-following, single-service simplicity) and propose a better-justified alternative.

sections.heading: The Question to Start From: How Will This Data Actually Be Read and Written?
sections.body:
Teams often choose a data store by asking 'which AWS database service should we use', which skips the part that determines the answer. Start instead from how the data will be queried and updated, at what volume, with what consistency requirements, and how much those access patterns vary or stay fixed over the system's lifetime. Only then ask which service's model matches. The answer is often 'it depends on the workload', which is more useful than 'the newest or most-discussed service is probably the right default'.

RDS, DynamoDB, and S3 aren't three implementations of one idea ranked by how modern or scalable they are. (AWS offers more stores for narrower jobs, such as ElastiCache for in-memory caching, OpenSearch for full-text search, and Redshift for analytics warehouses, but these three cover most first decisions.) They are built around different access-pattern assumptions, and using one where the workload calls for another causes specific pain. Forcing ad-hoc relational queries into DynamoDB leads to the expensive Scans from the previous concept, and forcing massive, predictable, key-addressed scale into RDS leads to instance-sizing and read-replica battles that DynamoDB's model was built to avoid.

sections.heading: RDS: When Query Flexibility and Strong Relational Guarantees Matter Most
sections.body:
RDS, a relational engine, is the right default when queries are varied and not fully known in advance, when the data has rich relationships across entities that are queried together (a reporting system that joins orders, customers, and products in ad-hoc ways), or when strong transactional guarantees across related writes are a hard requirement (a multi-table `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` that succeeds or fails as one unit; moving money between two accounts is the canonical example). A relational query planner with its indexing and join machinery makes a wide range of query shapes reasonably efficient without redesigning the schema each time a new need appears, which is the flexibility DynamoDB's access-pattern-first design trades away for its scaling properties.

RDS's cost shows up at very high, predictable scale. A single instance has a ceiling on write throughput (mitigated, not eliminated, by a bigger instance class or by Aurora's more scalable storage), and read scaling means adding and managing read replicas, as covered earlier, with no transparent scale-out like DynamoDB's partition model. For varied, evolving query needs that trade is worth it. For a few fixed, extremely high-volume access patterns known in advance, it is a price paid for flexibility the workload may never use.

sections.heading: DynamoDB: When Access Patterns Are Known and Scale Is the Priority
sections.body:
DynamoDB is the right default when access patterns are few, well understood in advance, and need a request volume or latency consistency that a relational engine would struggle to sustain without significant operational effort: a high-traffic session store, a shopping cart service, an IoT device-state table taking constant writes from millions of devices, or counter-style workloads with very high, predictable volume against a small set of query shapes. (Global leaderboards need care, since a single 'top 100' key concentrates traffic; see the exercise.) Latency stays flat as the table grows for the access patterns its keys were designed around, and throughput scales without the instance sizing and replica management RDS requires. You pay for it in one of two capacity modes: on-demand (pay per request, no planning) or provisioned (you set read and write capacity units, optionally with auto scaling). Capacity units are concrete: one write unit covers one write of up to 1 KB per second, and one read unit covers one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second (or two eventually consistent reads), so 100 strongly consistent reads per second of 8 KB items need 100 x 2 = 200 read units.

The cost shows up when access patterns turn out less fixed than assumed: a new query that doesn't fit the existing keys or secondary indexes needs an expensive Scan, or a reshaped table (often a new secondary index, sometimes a restructured item design and a backfill). An exploratory workload, where the team doesn't yet know what questions it will ask, fights DynamoDB's core assumption from day one, and RDS's flexibility, or a hybrid of both stores, is usually the better starting point until the patterns stabilize.

sections.heading: S3: When the Unit of Access Is a Whole Object, Not a Row or an Item
sections.body:
S3, covered earlier, is neither a relational database nor a NoSQL key-value store, but it belongs in this comparison. When the natural unit of access is a whole file or blob (user-uploaded images and videos, PDF exports, large batch data files, logs, backups, archives), S3 is often the right store, not a fallback for when a 'real' database doesn't fit. S3 has no query language beyond fetching by key or listing by prefix, so it can't replace RDS or DynamoDB when you need to query, filter, or join structured fields. (Services such as Athena and S3 Select can query file contents, but they are analytics tools, not a transactional lookup path.) It is the clear choice when the pattern is 'store this blob, retrieve it later by key, at large scale and low per-GB cost.'

A common, reasonable architecture uses more than one store for the same feature, each for the part it fits. An image-upload feature might keep the image bytes in S3, a DynamoDB item per upload for metadata and processing status keyed by upload ID (a fixed, high-volume, simple pattern), and RDS for the surrounding application data that benefits from joins and ad-hoc reporting, such as which users uploaded which images under which categories, queried flexibly by an admin dashboard. No store does another's job in that design.

sections.heading: A Framework, and a Warning Against Choosing by Trend
sections.body:
A workable framework asks, in order: First, is the unit of access a whole file or blob, or structured data with fields to query or filter? If a blob, S3 is very likely right for that part of the data. Second, for structured data, are the access patterns few, fixed, and known in advance, with a need for very high, predictable-latency scale (DynamoDB's strength), or are queries varied, evolving, or dependent on joins across entities not fully known up front (RDS's strength)? Third, does any part have a hard requirement for multi-row or multi-item transactional atomicity across different entities? That points toward RDS, or toward DynamoDB's narrower but real transaction support (`TransactWriteItems`) for limited cases.

Choosing a store because it is newest, most discussed, or the one the last project used, and only afterward trying to make the access patterns fit, reliably causes the pain described here: expensive Scans bolted onto a DynamoDB table never designed for the query someone eventually needed, or an RDS instance straining under a workload that was always simple, fixed, and enormous in volume. Understand the access pattern first, as specifically as possible, and let that, not trend, team familiarity alone, or a service's marketing, decide which store or combination fits.

examples.title: Same Feature, Three Data Stores Working Together
examples.code:
Feature: user-uploaded document processing pipeline

S3        -> stores the actual uploaded file bytes
             key: uploads/{userId}/{uploadId}.pdf

DynamoDB  -> tracks per-upload processing status, a fixed, high-volume,
             simple access pattern ("get this upload's current status")
             partition key: uploadId
             attributes: status, uploadedAt, s3Key

RDS       -> stores user accounts, billing plans, and admin-facing
             reporting joins ("which users on the Pro plan uploaded
             more than 10 files last month, grouped by category")
             tables: users, billing_plans, upload_metadata (foreign key to uploadId)
examples.explanation: Each store handles the part of the workload its strengths match. S3 holds the file bytes because that is pure blob storage with no field-level querying. DynamoDB holds per-upload status because 'look up this upload's status by ID' is a fixed, extremely high-volume, single-item pattern, a poor fit for RDS at large upload volume since you would be sizing a relational instance for a giant key-value lookup. RDS holds the account, billing, and reporting data because the admin query (filter by plan, group by category, join users to uploads) is the varied, join-heavy pattern RDS is built for, and it would need an expensive Scan or substantial redesign in DynamoDB.

examples.title: The Same Access Pattern, Forced Into the Wrong Store
examples.code:
Workload: ad-hoc, evolving analytics -- "show me all orders over $500 placed
 by customers in California, grouped by product category, for any date
 range a business analyst picks in a dashboard tool"

Forced into DynamoDB:
  -> no partition key maps to "any date range, any state, any amount
     threshold, any category" -- this is a different, unpredictable
     filter combination every time an analyst uses the dashboard
  -> every such query falls back to an expensive Scan across the
     whole Orders table, reading far more data than it returns

Correctly placed in RDS:
  -> SELECT category, SUM(total) FROM orders
     JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
     WHERE customers.state = 'CA' AND orders.total > 500
       AND orders.order_date BETWEEN :start AND :end
     GROUP BY category;
  -> the query planner and appropriate indexes handle this efficiently
     without needing the exact filter combination to be known in advance
examples.explanation: This is the access pattern DynamoDB's model is not built for: an ad-hoc combination of filters across several attributes and a related table (customers), chosen differently by an analyst each time, with no small set of known query shapes to design a partition key around. Each filter combination would need its own key design or secondary index to avoid a Scan, which isn't realistic for open-ended analytics. RDS handles it because the SQL states the filter and join logic and the planner finds an execution plan without the schema having been designed for this exact combination. (For truly large analytics, a columnar warehouse or Athena over S3 would be the next step, but the RDS-versus-DynamoDB point stands.) Fixed, known, high-volume patterns favor DynamoDB; varied, evolving, join-dependent ones favor RDS.

examples.title: Recognizing a Trend-Driven Choice and Correcting It
examples.code:
Original reasoning: "DynamoDB is what modern, scalable teams use, so we built our
 new internal admin tool's data model on it."

Actual workload: a handful of internal staff, low request volume, and every
 week someone needs a genuinely new report -- filtered and grouped in ways
 nobody anticipated when the table was designed.

Symptom: every new report request means either a new secondary index (a
 real, recurring engineering task) or an accepted expensive Scan, for a
 workload with low overall traffic that never actually needed DynamoDB's
 scaling properties in the first place.

Corrected reasoning: low request volume + constantly evolving, unpredictable
 query needs -> RDS's query flexibility is the better fit; DynamoDB's
 scaling strength was never the actual bottleneck this workload had.
examples.explanation: The original choice was wrong not because DynamoDB is a bad service but because the justification never engaged with this workload's access patterns. 'Modern, scalable teams use it' describes the service's reputation, not whether this tool's traffic or query variability calls for it. A low-traffic internal tool never stresses DynamoDB's scaling advantages, but it regularly stresses what DynamoDB trades away, flexible and unanticipated query shapes, and the team pays for that repeatedly in index maintenance or slow Scans. The corrected reasoning applies the framework: low volume and high query variability point at RDS. The lesson is not that DynamoDB was a mistake in general, but that this workload's pattern was never the one DynamoDB rewards.

misconceptions.description: DynamoDB is the newer, more scalable service, so it's generally the safer or more future-proof default choice for a new project's primary data store, even before considering the project's specific access patterns.
misconceptions.clarification: Scalability and query flexibility are a trade-off, not a strict improvement in DynamoDB's favor. DynamoDB rewards a small number of access patterns known in advance and penalizes ad-hoc or evolving needs with expensive Scans or index rework, while RDS's planner handles varied, unanticipated queries far more gracefully, at the cost of more deliberate scaling effort at very high volume. Neither is universally safer: the right default depends on whether the workload's access patterns are fixed and known (DynamoDB) or varied and evolving (RDS).

misconceptions.description: A well-architected system should pick exactly one data store and use it for everything, since using multiple different data stores for one feature adds unnecessary complexity.
misconceptions.clarification: Using more than one data store for a feature is normal, and often simpler overall, when its parts have different access patterns. File bytes, a fixed high-volume status lookup, and an evolving relational reporting query are three different problems, and forcing them into one store means accepting its weaknesses for whichever part doesn't fit. The complexity cost of operating several stores is real and worth weighing, but 'one store for everything' isn't simpler if it means fighting a mismatched pattern somewhere.

exercises.prompt: For each of the following three workloads, choose RDS, DynamoDB, or S3 as the primary store and justify the choice in one or two sentences based on its actual access pattern: (1) a video-streaming service's catalog of uploaded video files themselves; (2) a mobile game's leaderboard, read and written millions of times per minute by a fixed "get top 100" and "update this player's score" pair of operations; (3) a finance team's ad-hoc reporting tool where analysts write new, varied SQL-style queries against transaction data every week.
hints: For workload 1, ask what the unit of access is: a whole file, or individual structured fields within it?
For workload 2, note that both operations described ("get top 100", "update this score") are fixed and known in advance, at very high volume -- which store rewards that profile specifically?

For workload 3, the defining trait is that the queries themselves change every week and aren't known in advance -- which store's query engine is built to handle that kind of variability without redesigning storage each time?
exercises.solutionCode:
workload_1: S3
  reason: "The unit of access is the whole video file itself, retrieved by key at large scale and low per-GB cost -- there's no need to query individual fields within the file."

workload_2: DynamoDB
  reason: "Both access patterns are fixed, simple, and known in advance, at very high volume, which is the profile DynamoDB's partition-key model scales for. Caveat: 'get top 100' over all players needs a deliberate design, such as sharded leaderboard keys merged at read time, or an in-memory sorted set in ElastiCache or MemoryDB for the ranking, because one leaderboard key is a hot partition."

workload_3: RDS
  reason: "Query needs are ad-hoc and change weekly in ways not known in advance -- exactly the varied, evolving access pattern a relational query planner and indexing are built to handle, versus DynamoDB, which would require a new access pattern (and likely a new index or Scan) for every new report shape."
exercises.solutionExplanation: Each answer follows from the workload's access pattern, not from the service names. Workload 1's unit of access is an entire file with no field-level querying, which is S3's strength and an awkward fit for RDS (large blobs inside rows are generally discouraged) or DynamoDB (items are limited to 400 KB, far below a typical video). Workload 2's operations, a per-player score update and a top-100 read, are the small, fixed, very high-volume pattern DynamoDB is designed around, and flat latency as the leaderboard grows is what it needs. The per-player update maps cleanly onto a partition key of `playerId`. The global top-100 read is the tricky part: one leaderboard key would be a hot partition, so use sharded keys merged at read time or a purpose-built ranking structure alongside, and DynamoDB remains the best fit of the three for the write path. Workload 3's new, unanticipated query shapes every week are what DynamoDB structurally struggles with, since each needs a pre-designed access pattern or a Scan; RDS's planner and indexing handle that variability as a matter of course.

exercises.prompt: A team built their entire e-commerce backend -- product catalog, orders, customer accounts, AND an admin reporting dashboard with ad-hoc filtering -- as a single DynamoDB table, reasoning that using one store everywhere keeps the architecture simple. The admin dashboard now requires a new Scan-based query almost every time a manager asks for a new report filter, and each new filter combination risks becoming slow as the table grows. Diagnose the architectural mismatch and propose a better-justified design.
exercises.code:
current_design:
  store: DynamoDB (single table for everything)
  workloads:
    - product_catalog_lookup: "fixed access pattern, high volume"
    - order_placement_and_status: "fixed access pattern, high volume"
    - admin_reporting: "ad-hoc filters, changes almost weekly"
  symptom: "admin reporting keeps needing new Scans or new indexes; each new filter risks poor performance as data grows"
hints: Not every workload under this one team's backend actually has the same access-pattern profile -- which of the three listed workloads doesn't match the fixed, known-in-advance pattern DynamoDB rewards?
"One store for everything" was chosen for architectural simplicity, but is the admin reporting workload actually simpler as a result, given the recurring Scan/index problem?
Consider a design where the two fixed, high-volume workloads keep using DynamoDB, and the workload with evolving, ad-hoc query needs uses a different store better suited to it.
exercises.solutionCode:
corrected_design:
  store_for_catalog_and_orders: DynamoDB
    reason: "fixed, known, high-volume access patterns -- exactly DynamoDB's strength, unchanged from before"
  store_for_admin_reporting: RDS
    reason: "ad-hoc, evolving filter needs -- matches a relational query planner far better than repeated new Scans/indexes"
  data_flow: "order and catalog events stream (e.g. via DynamoDB Streams) into the RDS reporting store, kept eventually consistent for reporting purposes"
exercises.solutionExplanation: 'One store for everything' assumed all three workloads shared one access-pattern profile, when only two (catalog lookups and order placement/status) have the fixed, known, high-volume shape DynamoDB rewards. The admin reporting workload is the opposite: new filter combinations on a recurring basis keep forcing new Scans or indexes onto the table, and they get slower and more burdensome as data grows. The simplicity of one store was illusory for this workload once the recurring Scan and index churn is counted as ongoing cost. The corrected design keeps DynamoDB exactly where it was already working well (catalog and orders) and moves the reporting workload to RDS, where ad-hoc, evolving queries are a core strength rather than a recurring fight against the store's design. A common way to keep both stores in sync is streaming changes from DynamoDB (DynamoDB Streams, typically consumed by a Lambda function) into the RDS reporting store, accepting some lag in exchange for reporting queries that don't force a redesign of the transactional table each time a manager asks a new question. For heavier analytics, exporting the table to S3 and querying it with Athena is another option.

assessments.prompt: A team is building a service that ingests sensor readings from 2 million IoT devices, each writing a new reading roughly once per second, with the only required query being "fetch the latest N readings for one specific device ID." Which data store best fits this workload, and why?
options: DynamoDB, because the access pattern (fetch readings for one known device ID) is fixed, simple, and needs to sustain extremely high, predictable-latency write volume across a huge number of distinct partition key values.
Either RDS or DynamoDB works equally well here, since the query is simple enough that the choice makes no real difference at this scale.
RDS, because relational databases provide the strongest consistency guarantees, which any database workload should default to unless proven otherwise.
S3, because storing each reading as an individual object is the cheapest possible way to persist high-volume data regardless of query needs.
assessments.explanation: This workload is close to a textbook DynamoDB fit: the access pattern is fixed and known (fetch recent readings for one device ID, with `deviceId` as a natural high-cardinality partition key across 2 million devices and a timestamp sort key), and the write volume (2 million devices at roughly one write per second each) is extremely high and needs flat, predictable latency, which DynamoDB's partition model is designed to sustain without the instance sizing RDS would need. (At about 2 million writes per second, real capacity quotas and cost would need checking; the point here is the fit, not the bill.) The “RDS, because relational databases provide the strongest…” option's blanket 'default to strongest consistency' reasoning ignores that this workload never actually needed multi-row relational transactions or ad-hoc joins in the first place. The “S3, because storing each reading…” option misreads the requirement -- 'fetch the latest N readings for one device' is a query need S3 has no mechanism for at all beyond fetching by exact key; S3 would require pairing with an actual queryable index to serve this, not solve it alone. The “Either RDS or DynamoDB works equally well…” option is wrong because the scale and access-pattern profile described are specifically the case where the choice matters a great deal -- DynamoDB avoids an operational scaling battle that RDS would face at 2 million devices writing roughly every second.

assessments.prompt: A team needs to guarantee that a transfer between two bank accounts either fully succeeds (both the debit and the credit are applied) or fully fails with neither applied, even under concurrent access from other transfers. Which store's core strength most directly addresses this requirement?
options: DynamoDB, because its partition key design automatically guarantees atomicity across any two items in a table.
S3, because object versioning provides atomic multi-object updates across any two objects by default.

Any of the three stores handles this equally well, since atomicity is entirely a property of the application code and not something the underlying data store provides, so the choice should be made purely on price and on which of them the team has already used before.

RDS, because a relational engine's transactional guarantees -- committing or rolling back multiple related writes as a single atomic unit -- are specifically built for exactly this kind of multi-row, all-or-nothing requirement.
